title: Jean Baudrillard
summary: Jean Baudrillard was a French sociologist and philosopher who studied consumer society and the media. His central idea: images and copies increasingly replace reality — these are “simulacra,” copies without an original — until “hyperreality” emerges, a world where the image seems more real than the world itself. He wrote provocatively and rather darkly, but his view helps you notice how much of what you feel has been shaped by screens and shop windows.
onEmotions: Baudrillard built no theory of emotions and was skeptical of “psychology.” But an important thought follows from his ideas: many feelings today pass through simulacra — images of happiness from advertising, rehearsed emotions on social media, the “right” feelings from TV series. In The Consumer Society he showed that we buy things as signs of status and identity, not only for their use — and the same happens with moods. His view is uncomfortable, but freeing: if your feeling doesn't match the glossy picture, perhaps it is the picture that is wrong, not you. It is worth looking not for the “ideal” emotion but for the one that remains when the screen is switched off.

anxiety.text: Anxiety with no clear cause is one of the most common experiences of our time, and you are not alone in it. Baudrillard described the modern world as an “ecstasy of communication”: everything becomes visible, everything is available, the flow of messages never stops. In such an environment a person loses their protective distance — they become a “screen” through which other people's news, opinions and disasters pass. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that part of your anxiety is not a personal malfunction but a natural reaction to a surplus of signals that cannot be digested. This doesn't mean your anxiety is “not real.” But it helps to tell apart the anxiety about what is happening to you and the anxiety the screen brings. The second kind can sometimes be eased simply by closing the flow for a while.
anxiety.practice: Count how many alarming messages you have seen in the last hour. Then put your phone aside for five minutes and ask yourself: what is worrying me here, in this room?

fear.text: Fear is an ancient protector, and it deserves respect. But Baudrillard paid attention to how modern media work with fear. Disasters and threats are shown so often and so spectacularly that they become “hyperreality” — an image that feels more real than the everyday life outside your window. Baudrillard also wrote about the logic of “deterrence”: modern systems rest less on events than on their constant possibility, always looming on the horizon. From his point of view, you could say that we live through many fears “in simulation” — again and again, before anything has actually happened. Recognizing this doesn't mean dismissing the danger. It helps you return to the concrete: what threatens me in particular, right now, and what is within my power?
fear.practice: Split your fear into two parts: what you have seen with your own eyes, and what you have only seen on a screen or heard secondhand. Which part weighs more?

sadness.text: Sadness sometimes descends for no visible reason — and that doesn't make you “ungrateful” or “weak.” Baudrillard considered melancholy the basic mood of the age of simulation: when meanings multiply, get copied and lose their value, there seems to be more of everything around — and less of anything real. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that your sadness may be a sensitive response not only to something personal but to this shared “faded” atmosphere, where even feelings come prepackaged. That doesn't make sadness an illness. It is more a sign of living receptiveness. Baudrillard writes no prescriptions for cheerfulness — he suggests not pretending. Allowing yourself to be sad without a “positive” filter is already a small way out of the simulation.
sadness.practice: Describe your sadness in one sentence you would never post on social media. How does the feeling sound without a filter?

grief.text: Grief is a heavy and entirely legitimate response to loss; there is nothing in it that needs “fixing.” In Symbolic Exchange and Death Baudrillard notices something important about our culture: modern society pushes loss to the margins — hides it, hurries it, gives it less and less room in shared life. In traditional cultures, he says, the living continued an “exchange” with the departed: through rituals, gifts, memory, conversation. We, by contrast, often expect a grieving person to “get back to normal” quickly. From Baudrillard's point of view, your grief doesn't have to adapt to that pace. You can keep a bond with whoever or whatever you have lost: remember, talk, make small ritual gestures. This is not weakness but a recovery of something our culture has forgotten how to do.
grief.practice: Come up with one small personal ritual of remembrance — lighting a candle, writing a few lines, walking a familiar route. What would you like to “say” to what you have lost today?

loneliness.text: Loneliness is especially painful when there seems to be endless communication all around. Baudrillard described this as the paradox of the “ecstasy of communication”: connections multiply, messages fly nonstop, but the encounter itself — presence, silence shared by two, a look — is more and more often replaced by its simulation. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that a reaction under a post resembles attention, a chat resembles a conversation, a feed resembles your friends' lives. And your loneliness may be not a sign that something is wrong with you, but an accurate sense of the difference between the sign of closeness and closeness itself. That sense is a valuable sensitivity. It suggests that what you need is not another portion of contact, but a different kind of it — slow, bodily, imperfect, without an audience.
loneliness.practice: Remember the last conversation that left you feeling warmer. How was it different from messaging? Could you repeat even something of it this week?

anger.text: Anger is an honest energy, and it has its reasons. Baudrillard saw one of the most infuriating features of the modern world: the system knows how to absorb protest and hand it back as a commodity. A rebel symbol becomes a T-shirt print, critique becomes content, outrage becomes a reason to click. Hence a particular anger with no outlet: it seems that even your rage has already been built into someone's shop window. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say it isn't worth handing your anger over to be recycled into yet another spectacle. He himself responded to the world with irony and provocation rather than head-on confrontation. You can acknowledge anger, feel it in your body and direct it into a real conversation or action — where it changes something, rather than just collecting views.
anger.practice: Ask yourself: who or what is my anger really addressed to? Write down one small real action that would make it heard, not just displayed.

shame.text: Shame about your body, your appearance, your way of life is a very common and painful feeling, and it is not your fault that you feel it. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard called the body “the finest consumer object”: the body is turned into a project to be constantly improved, invested in, displayed. The standards, meanwhile, are set by edited images — simulacra that have no living original. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that shame arises when a living, changing person compares themselves to a copy without an original. It is an unfair competition. Understanding this logic doesn't dissolve shame at once, but it changes its meaning: you are not “falling short” — you are measuring yourself against something that doesn't actually exist.
shame.practice: Think of an image next to which you feel ashamed. Ask: does this person or this life really exist — without the lighting, retouching and editing?

guilt.text: Guilt can come even when you haven't harmed anyone — for instance, for not being happy, productive or “positive” enough. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard wrote about “fun-morality” (he used the English phrase): in a society of abundance, pleasure becomes a duty. You are supposed to enjoy yourself, try new things, rest “properly” — and if it doesn't work out, it feels as if you've broken a rule. From Baudrillard's point of view, such guilt is not the voice of conscience but the inner supervisor of consumer society. A simple question helps tell one from the other: whom have I harmed? If no one — perhaps you are “guilty” only before an advertising image of a happy life, and you owe it nothing.
guilt.practice: Write down what you blame yourself for. Next to it, answer: who specifically was hurt? If there is no answer, name whose rule you broke.

envy.text: Envy is unpleasant but deeply human — and to a large extent it is produced by the very environment we live in. In The System of Objects and The Consumer Society Baudrillard showed that we acquire things not only for their use but for their “sign value” — what they say about our place among others. A need, for Baudrillard, is often a need not for the thing itself but for difference: to be no worse, to be more visible. Such a system is never satisfied, because a new mark of distinction will always appear. From his point of view, envy is not your moral flaw but a programmed effect of this race. Once the mechanism is visible, envy becomes less personal, and you can ask: what do I really want, and what is merely a sign for standing out?
envy.practice: Write down the object of your envy and ask: if no one ever found out I had it, would I still want it?

emptiness.text: Emptiness is no small thing: it can feel like life itself has lost its taste. Baudrillard offered an unexpected explanation for this feeling. In Simulacra and Simulation he describes a world where copies, images and models gradually push reality aside, leaving “the desert of the real” — there is a lot of everything, yet nothing truly touches you. We are surrounded by pictures of food, travel, love, and it is their very excess that can leave us hungry. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that your emptiness may be an honest response to life among simulacra — and so evidence that you need something real. It is not a verdict but a compass. The real is usually humbler than the image: a warm cup in your hands, a living voice, footsteps on a street.
emptiness.practice: Right now, find one sensation that can't be photographed: the temperature of the air, the weight of your body, a sound. Stay with it for a minute.

confusion.text: Confusion is a natural response to a world that changes faster than we can understand it. Baudrillard wrote about the “implosion of meaning” in the media (an implosion is an explosion directed inward): there is more and more information, but instead of clarifying meaning it dissolves it. Every event immediately gathers a thousand interpretations, refutations and jokes — and it is no longer clear what actually happened. From Baudrillard's point of view, your confusion is not a sign of stupidity or of being unable to cope. It is a reasonable response to an environment where the line between the real and its image is blurred. What helps may be not more information but less: relying on what you know from your own experience, and the right to say, “I don't know yet, and that's okay.”
confusion.practice: Pick a question that confuses you and write down only what you know about it firsthand. How much is left?

quote.text: We live in a world where there is more and more information, and less and less meaning.
quote.author: Jean Baudrillard
quote.source: Simulacra and Simulation (1981), “The Implosion of Meaning in the Media”

fatigue.text: Fatigue and burnout are not a sign of weakness. Remarkably, as early as 1970, in The Consumer Society, Baudrillard devoted several pages to tiredness. He noticed that in the society of abundance a strange, “causeless” fatigue spreads, one that physical labor cannot explain. And he offered a bold reading: such fatigue may be a hidden form of resistance — a quiet, bodily refusal of constant mobilization, of the demand to keep producing, consuming and staying on top form. From this point of view, your burnout is not only a personal failure but a signal your body sends instead of words: “I can't go on like this.” That signal deserves to be heard, not drowned out by yet another “efficient” recovery technique.
fatigue.practice: Ask your fatigue: what exactly is it refusing? Write down one demand you could lift from yourself, at least partly, this week.

boredom.text: Boredom seems trivial, but it can be very heavy — especially amid endless entertainment. Baudrillard described our time as the state “after the orgy”: everything has already been liberated, permitted, made available, shown — and that is precisely why desire loses its tension. When any film and any music are in your pocket, choosing stops being exciting. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that boredom is not your shortcoming but a natural effect of oversaturation. Treating it with even more content is useless — it only prolongs the “after the orgy.” Sometimes boredom asks for the opposite: limits, pauses, mystery. What isn't available right away becomes interesting again. In this sense boredom is not an emptiness inside you, but desire's longing for the distance that was taken from it.
boredom.practice: Choose one thing — a film, an album, a book — and set it aside until tomorrow without opening it. Notice how your attitude to it changes while you wait.

quote.text: If I were asked to characterize the present state of affairs, I would describe it as “after the orgy.”
quote.author: Jean Baudrillard

joy.text: Joy is precious, and it needs neither proof nor justification. Baudrillard criticized the “happiness industry” a great deal — advertising smiles, compulsory leisure, joy as a commodity. But he was no enemy of pleasure. In Seduction he contrasts the world of production, where everything must yield a result, with the world of play, appearances, ritual and lightness. Seduction, for Baudrillard, is a game in which nothing needs to be accumulated or proven. From his point of view, you could say that real joy is closer to play than to achievement. It doesn't have to become a photo, a post or a “result.” Let your joy stay a little unproductive and a little secret — that way it stays yours for longer.
joy.practice: Live through one joy today without showing it or telling anyone about it. How is it different from a joy that gets shared?

love.text: Love and tenderness are among our most alive feelings. Baudrillard defended them in an unexpected way — through the value of secrecy. He criticized the culture of total transparency, where everything must be shown, spelled out, put on display; he called such transparency “obscene,” because it destroys the distance in which desire lives. In Seduction he writes about the play of appearances and things left unsaid, about the fact that the other is never fully revealed. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that tenderness needs a little shadow. Not every feeling has to be explained and published. Your love doesn't become smaller because others don't see it; sometimes it is precisely secrecy that keeps it alive.
love.practice: Recall a small gesture of tenderness that only you and the other person know about. What does it mean to you?

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a warm feeling that carries a sense of the gift. Drawing on the anthropologist Marcel Mauss, Baudrillard contrasted commodity exchange with “symbolic exchange”: gift and counter-gift, a bond that can't be reduced to a price. In the commodity world everything can be bought and returned, and once accounts are settled nobody owes anybody anything. In symbolic exchange, a gift creates a relationship and a continuation. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that gratitude is a small exit from the logic of the market. When you give thanks not for a service but for presence, attention, for what cannot be paid for, you restore to yourself and to the other the part of life that isn't for sale. It is enough to answer such a gift — with a word, with time, with a small gesture.
gratitude.practice: Recall something you were given that can't be paid for. What small gift in return — a word, a gesture, some time — could you offer?

hope.text: Hope can seem naive in a world that Baudrillard described so darkly. But he has an unexpectedly encouraging thought. In The Perfect Crime he writes about “the murder of reality” — the attempt to replace the world with its flawless, fully calculated copy. And he notes that this crime is never perfect. Traces, accidents, illusions always remain — something that slips out of control. The world does not yield to total simulation. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that hope lives precisely in these remainders — in the unpredictable, in what fits neither a forecast nor an algorithm. Not everything is decided in advance. Reality resists, and this stubbornness of the world is a good foundation for hope.
hope.practice: Remember a time when something didn't go to plan — and turned out unexpectedly better. What does that say about how predetermined your future is?

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a tender, aching feeling, and it is understandable. Baudrillard noticed that in the age of simulation nostalgia becomes especially strong: as reality is increasingly replaced by copies, we are drawn to what once seemed authentic. Hence the fashion for “retro,” vintage filters, endless reissues — the past, too, becomes a commodity and an image. From Baudrillard's point of view, you can distinguish two nostalgias: a bought one — for a stylized “past” that never existed — and a living one — for particular people, places, smells. The first is easy to manipulate. The second is honest and speaks of your values. Don't be ashamed of nostalgia — just ask: do I miss what actually was, or a beautiful picture of it?
nostalgia.practice: Take one nostalgic memory and remove its “filter”: what ordinary, uncomfortable details were there too? What stays precious even with them?

quote.text: When the real is no longer what it used to be, nostalgia assumes its full meaning.
quote.author: Jean Baudrillard
quote.source: Simulacra and Simulation (1981), “The Precession of Simulacra”

craving.text: A sharp “I want it right now” — for a cigarette, a drink, your phone — can be almost unbearable, and there is nothing shameful in it. In The System of Objects Baudrillard described the collector's passion: what keeps a collection moving is not the object already found, but the one still missing. The last item is always ahead — and so desire never closes. In The Consumer Society he added that we want not only the thing but what it signifies — its “sign value”: calm, freedom, belonging, a pause. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that a craving often promises not the thing itself but a sign the thing can never fully deliver anyway. This doesn't make the craving weaker, but it changes the question. Not “how do I defeat it,” but “what sign am I trying to get right now — and is there another way to it?” Meanwhile the wave of craving rises and falls, even if you don't feed it.
craving.practice: When a wave of craving comes, finish the sentence: “What I actually want right now is…” — and name not the thing, but what it means to you.

addiction.text: When life has been built around one thing for years — a substance, gambling, a screen — it is very hard to step out of that circle, and it isn't about “weak willpower.” Baudrillard showed that consumer society works as an endless system of signs: every purchase points to the next, and none brings things to a close, because desire here is aimed not at the object but at difference and promise. Consumption, for Baudrillard, knows no satiation by its very logic. From his point of view, you could say that addiction is the same mechanism pushed to its limit and compressed into a single object. It says nothing about you being corrupt; it says how powerfully built the trap is that a great many people fall into. Against this logic Baudrillard set “symbolic exchange” — relationships of the gift, which bind people rather than things. Sometimes the way out of the circle begins exactly like that: with a living connection rather than one more sign.
addiction.practice: Think of someone around whom you feel even a little lighter. You could simply write them a few words — or, if you feel like it, look for a mutual-help group where people talk about the same thing without judgment.

hangover.text: The morning after — with heaviness in your body, anxiety and gaps in your memory — is a very uncomfortable state, and it doesn't make you a bad person. Baudrillard wrote about our era as the state “after the orgy,” but his thought has a more everyday side too: today events almost always leave a double behind — photos, videos, messages. In the morning it often seems these copies know more about your evening than you do, and your memory gets pieced together from other people's shots. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that such a “record” is not the same as what happened. A snapshot tears a second out of context, and anxiety adds the worst possible story to it. You don't have to accept this hyperreal version as the final truth about yourself. You can let your body recover and return to the real: what you know for sure, whom it might be worth calmly messaging, and what is only a picture inflated by shame.
hangover.practice: Divide a sheet into two columns: “what I know for sure” and “what I'm filling in.” For now, just look at which column is longer.

euphoria.text: A sudden high, when everything seems possible, is a bright and pleasant experience, and you can simply enjoy it. Baudrillard distinguished two ways in which things go beyond their limits. One he called “ecstasy” — in Fatal Strategies, a movement that spins on its own, faster and faster, until it loses meaning. The other is “seduction”: play, lightness, appearance, in which nothing needs to be accumulated or proven. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that a flash of euphoria is better lived as seduction than as ecstasy — as play rather than as an obligation to keep speeding up. You don't need to turn it into a post, a proof or a plan for the rest of your life. Let it be what it is: a gift of the moment, with a beginning and an end. That is exactly why it is so good.
euphoria.practice: Describe this high in three words no one will see. What about it is dear to you right now, without plans for tomorrow?

crash.text: The drop after a high — after a celebration, a success, a vivid evening — can be sharp and hurtful: a moment ago everything was so good, and now it all seems faded. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard described the logic of fashion: signs of success and celebration flare up, quickly lose their value and demand replacement. A party, a holiday, an achievement are often lived as such signs — and a sign, for Baudrillard, is short-lived and leaves behind an emptiness that you are immediately offered to fill with something new. From his point of view, you could say that the “comedown” is not proof that the joy was fake or that something is wrong with you. It is the moment when the sign has gone out, and life goes on. There's no need to rush to drown the drop with a new high. You can give yourself an ordinary, quiet day — with no celebration and no verdict.
crash.practice: Name one entirely ordinary thing that is still good today: tea, the light in the window, someone's voice. Stay with it for a minute.

panic.text: A wave of panic is one of the most frightening experiences: your heart, your breathing, the sense that something irreparable is about to happen. It is genuinely terrifying, and you are not exaggerating. Baudrillard described the person of the age of the “ecstasy of communication” as a being without protective distance: everything comes too close, everything gets inside, personal space seems to vanish. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that in panic the world and the body are experienced exactly like this — with no gap, no “frame,” everything at once and right up close. That's why what helps is whatever restores even a little distance and concreteness: not the image of catastrophe your mind is painting, but the tangible reality around you — the floor, the chair, the air. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. While it lasts, it is enough to hold on to the simplest, most real things.
panic.practice: Place both feet on the floor and take a few slow breaths, making each exhale longer than the inhale. Name out loud five objects you can see.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is all this for,” the sense of finitude and the abyss — is heavy, and many thoughtful people know it. Baudrillard was a dark thinker, but his later books, such as The Perfect Crime and The Vital Illusion, offer an unexpected foothold. He believed the world never reduces to a final meaning, and he called this the “radical illusion” of the world: reality is not transparent; mystery always remains in it. For him this was not a catastrophe but the condition of being alive: a world fully explained and calculated would be a dead copy. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that the question “what for” gets no final answer not because everything is meaningless, but because the world is larger than any answer. The abyss is this very inexhaustibility. You can look at it not only with fear but with curiosity.
dread.practice: Write down one thing in the world that amazes you and that you can't fully explain. Stay with that amazement for a minute.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives and you are missing something important is painful and very widespread. Baudrillard gave this feeling a precise language. The feed is a shop window of “hyperreality”: there life appears in selected, edited, spliced-together shots, and those shots seem more real than your own weekdays. For Baudrillard, a simulacrum doesn't necessarily lie — it simply takes the place of what was and begins to set the standard. From his point of view, you could say that you are comparing your life from the inside with someone else's life as a sign. It's an unfair comparison from the start — the backstage always loses to the shop window. Your life isn't worse; it just hasn't been edited. And the evening you are “missing” was an ordinary evening for the people there too — with boredom, fatigue and awkwardness that didn't make it into the frame.
fomo.practice: Recall a post or photo of your own that looked better than things really were. What stayed out of frame?

sleepless.text: Insomnia and 3 a.m. thoughts are exhausting, and in the dark everything seems bigger and scarier. Baudrillard wrote that the modern person lives in a state of constant connection: the screen never goes dark, the flow never stops, and the difference between day and night, work and rest, gets erased. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that the night could be the last place without signals, but often the screen takes it over too — the feed, the news, unfinished messages. And thoughts in the dark work like the same flow: they replay scenarios that haven't happened and perhaps never will — simulations of the future. You don't need to defeat them. You can just notice that this is replaying, not reality, and give the night back at least a little of its own darkness and quiet.
sleepless.practice: If you can't sleep, turn your phone face down and feel the weight of the blanket and the pillow. Tell yourself: “This is just replaying; morning will sort it out.”

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only trust in a person but the sense that the world is reliable. Following the anthropologist Marcel Mauss, Baudrillard described “symbolic exchange” — relationships held together by gift and response, trust and obligation, which can't be reduced to a transaction. In such relationships every gesture means something and calls for an answer. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that betrayal hurts so much precisely because it destroys a symbolic bond, not merely breaks a contract. You gave what cannot be paid for — time, openness, loyalty — and the gift in return never came. Your pain is an accurate measure of the value of what you invested. It says nothing about you being naive. The capacity for symbolic exchange is not a weakness but what makes us human, and there's no need to cancel it because of one rupture.
betrayal.practice: Write down what exactly you gave in this relationship — things that can't be bought. That remains yours, even if there was no answer.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a burning and very human feeling: the fear of losing someone dear. Baudrillard wrote a great deal about how our culture demands total transparency: everything must be visible, checked, shown. He called such transparency “obscene,” because it destroys distance, and with it mystery and seduction. In Seduction he insists that another person is never fully revealed, and that this is exactly what makes them desirable. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that jealousy often pushes toward obscene transparency — to check, to find out, to see everything. But complete visibility brings no peace: behind every answer a new question appears. Accepting that the other is always partly a mystery is painful. But it also means accepting them as a living person, not an object that can be fully controlled.
jealousy.practice: Notice what “check” you want to do right now. Before doing it, ask yourself: what do I actually want to hear from this person?

resentment.text: An old grudge is like a weight you carry for years, and it is hard to let go of on command. In his late book Impossible Exchange Baudrillard writes about things that cannot be exchanged for any equivalent. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that resentment often rests on exactly this. We wait for compensation — an apology, recognition, punishment — that will balance out the harm done. But some wounds have no equivalent: no word will “give back” what happened. Hence the endless waiting that feeds the grudge. Accepting that the exchange is impossible is bitter, but it can free you: you stop waiting for a payment that won't come, and you no longer have to keep that account. This doesn't mean forgiving or excusing. It means ceasing to be a hostage to waiting and taking your attention back.
resentment.practice: Write down what “compensation” you are waiting for. Then ask: if it were certain never to come, what would I want to do for myself?

heartbreak.text: A broken heart hurts literally, in the body, and it takes time. Baudrillard noticed a feature of our era: everything leaves digital doubles behind. After a breakup a person disappears from your life, but their photos remain, your messages, a profile where life goes on without you. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that you are grieving a real person while also running into their simulacrum, which keeps the loss from coming to an end. The image remains available, but the person does not. It isn't a weakness of yours that it's hard not to look: these copies are designed to draw you in. Often the kindest thing is to put the image at a little distance — not out of revenge and not forever, but so that the real loss can run its course and make room for new life.
heartbreak.practice: Choose one “trace” — a chat, a photo, a profile — and put it out of sight for at least a week, without deleting it. Notice what changes.

impostor.text: The fear that you are about to be exposed and everyone will realize you are “not the real thing” is very painful, and even highly competent people know it. In Simulacra and Simulation Baudrillard gives a curious example: someone who simulates an illness begins to produce some of its real symptoms — and the line between “true” and “false” blurs. His conclusion is broader: in the modern world, professional roles, statuses and competences largely exist as signs that everyone jointly maintains. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that the “real expert” you fear you can't measure up to has no inner original either — they too are playing a role and learning as they go. You are not the only pretender in a world of genuine people. You are a person doing the work, and your skill is real exactly to the extent that it works.
impostor.practice: Write down three things you actually did in the past month — just facts. They happened, even if you felt like an impostor.

self_hatred.text: When your inner critic says you do everything wrong and that you yourself are “not right,” it hurts a great deal, and its verdict is not the truth. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard described how the body and personality are turned into a project to be endlessly improved, with the models for it set by advertising images — copies without a living original. In The Transparency of Evil he spoke of “the hell of the same” — a world where everyone is obliged to coincide with an ideal model of themselves. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that the inner critic often speaks in the voice of that model. It compares a living, contradictory person with a simulacrum that doesn't exist. In such a competition anyone would lose. Your failure to match the template is not proof that you are worthless, but a sign that you are real.
self_hatred.practice: Write down one sentence from your inner critic and ask: whose voice is this, and what picture is it measuring me against? Then add the sentence a kind friend would say to you.

helplessness.text: Feeling powerless to change anything is hard to bear, especially when you are trying very hard. Baudrillard was skeptical of the idea that an individual steers the world. In Fatal Strategies he suggested looking from the other side: it is not the subject who rules over objects; the world, events and things live by their own logic, and often everything goes differently from what was planned. For Baudrillard this is not a reason for despair but a sobering truth. From his point of view, you could say that your helplessness is largely an honest perception of scale, not a personal failure. Not everything depends on you, and the weight of “I must fix everything” can be eased a little. At the same time the world is unpredictable in both directions: what seems frozen sometimes shifts unexpectedly. Your task is not to control everything but to stay alert to the moment when something becomes possible.
helplessness.practice: Divide the situation into two parts: “not in my power” and “a little bit in my power.” Pick one small thing from the second for today.

procrastination.text: When you can't get started even though you really need to, it's easy to start blaming yourself. In The Mirror of Production Baudrillard criticized the notion that a human being is essentially a producer whose value is measured by output. This idea sits so deep in us that we perceive any pause as failure. In The Consumer Society he observed that even rest becomes a duty and a form of working on yourself. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that procrastination is sometimes not laziness but a quiet bodily “no” to endless mobilization. That doesn't mean the task is unimportant. But if you take off it the weight of being “proof of your worth,” starting often becomes easier. The task is just a task, not a trial of you. You can do a small, ugly, imperfect part of it.
procrastination.practice: Do the smallest and least important part of the task — open the file, write one clumsy line — and let it be bad.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — after emigration, a move, the loss of familiar ground — can run very deep: as if everything around is foreign and the old is already out of reach. Baudrillard traveled a lot and wrote America through the eyes of a foreigner. In The Transparency of Evil he recalls with sympathy the writer Victor Segalen and his idea of the “exote” — a traveler who is in no hurry to appropriate what is foreign, but learns to value its difference. For Baudrillard, strangeness is not only loss but also a rare experience of meeting something that can't be reduced to yourself. From his point of view, you could say that your foreignness in a new place is painful, but it also holds a sharpness of vision that locals have lost. You see what is invisible to them. You don't have to either dissolve into the new place or cling to the old one: for a while you can simply be in between.
uprooted.practice: Write down one strange or surprising detail of the new place that locals surely don't notice. What does it tell you?

overload.text: Overload from the endless feed, notifications and news is exhausting, and it isn't your inability to “cope.” Baudrillard described this state long before smartphones. He called it the “ecstasy of communication”: everything becomes visible, available, instant, and a person turns into a screen through which streams of messages pass. He called this excessive visibility “obscenity” — not in the sense of indecency but in the sense of the disappearance of any stage or distance. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that overload is a normal reaction of a living being to an environment without pauses. Baudrillard also noted the response of “the masses”: not answering, not absorbing, letting things pass by. Sometimes that is the most sensible defense. You don't need to keep up with everything; you can reclaim a stage and a distance — a place where things happen at your own pace.
overload.practice: Turn off notifications for at least an hour and notice what changes in your body. Which signal did you actually need?

unreality.text: The sense that the world or you yourself are somehow not quite real can be frightening and disorienting. Baudrillard is perhaps the philosopher who wrote most about a similar experience at the level of culture. In Simulacra and Simulation he describes “hyperreality”: a world where images, models and copies begin to precede reality itself. He recalls Borges's story of a map that grew as large as the empire, and turns it around: now the map precedes the territory. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that your sense of unreality is not necessarily strange — it resonates with how many people experience life among screens and copies. And yet for Baudrillard reality never disappears completely: traces remain, accidents, the body. You can return to them gently, through the simplest sensations.
unreality.practice: Touch a surface near you — a table, fabric, a wall — and silently name its temperature and texture. This sensation can't be copied.

quote.text: The territory no longer precedes the map, nor survives it. Henceforth, it is the map that precedes the territory.
quote.author: Jean Baudrillard
quote.source: Simulacra and Simulation (1981), “The Precession of Simulacra”

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling, and it is worth simply living through. Baudrillard, known as a critic of simulations, was also a passionate photographer. He said that in a good photograph the initiative seems to pass to the object itself: it is not we who impose meaning on the world; the world itself comes through and captures us. In America he described deserts as spaces of such scale that familiar meanings dissolve. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that awe is the moment when the world exceeds any image or sign, when no picture can contain it. It is the opposite of hyperreality: not a copy, but an encounter with something larger than you. Baudrillard would call it the world's “seduction.” You don't need to do anything with it — it is enough to let yourself be captured.
awe.practice: If you want to photograph what filled you with awe, first look at it for a minute without the camera. What did only your eyes see?

relief.text: Relief is a warm feeling, when tension lets go. You can simply enjoy it. Baudrillard wrote that we often live through events in advance — in images, forecasts, scenarios replayed in our heads — so that the threat becomes almost more real than reality itself. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that relief is the moment when this simulation of the future meets the present and turns out not to be the only possibility. And his thought from The Perfect Crime — that the world is never fully calculated — is especially fitting here: things may not follow the worst-case script. Relief shows how much energy you spent on waiting. Let your body feel that this tension can be released — that, too, is a small return to the real.
relief.practice: Breathe out deeply and notice where in your body something has let go. Remember that place — you can come back to it next time.

calm.text: Calm and peace are infrequent guests, and it's good to take care of them. Baudrillard described our world as a space of continuous communication, where everything must be said, shown, discussed. Against this background he valued what remains unsaid: mystery, silence, understatement, which he associated with seduction. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that calm is a state outside the “ecstasy of communication,” when nothing needs to be broadcast and nothing needs an answer. It demands no result and doesn't become a sign. That is exactly why it is so hard to show to others — and there's no need to. Let your calm stay a little secret. Its value lies not in how it looks but in how it feels.
calm.practice: Stay in this calm for a few minutes without writing anything down or telling anyone. Notice how the silence around you sounds.

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful feeling, when an idea seems to find you on its own. Baudrillard liked the thought that it is not only the subject who chooses the object; the object also “seduces” the subject: things, images, ideas draw us in by themselves and lead us off the usual path. He connected the very word “seduction” with the Latin se-ducere — “to lead aside.” From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that inspiration is exactly this kind of seduction, when you are led aside from your schedule and plan. It isn't production on a timetable; it is play. You don't have to turn it into a product right away or report on results. First you can simply follow it — wherever it leads. Inspiration lives in lightness, and it needs no immediate usefulness to be valuable.
inspiration.practice: Write the idea down the way it came — unevenly, without polishing. Don't judge it today.

schadenfreude.text: A sudden pleasure at someone else's failure is familiar to almost everyone, and it doesn't make you a bad person. In The Transparency of Evil Baudrillard writes about “the principle of Evil”: a society that demands constant positivity, agreement and smiles from everyone cannot abolish the negative. It represses it, and then the negative returns in unexpected, strange forms. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that schadenfreude is one of these returns. A world where everyone must look successful and rejoice at others' successes in the feed accumulates hidden tension, and someone else's failure discharges it for a moment. Understanding this doesn't justify cruelty, but it removes some of the shame: your reaction is partly born of an environment of glossy competition. You can notice it without turning it into an action and without punishing yourself for the flash itself.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “Whose ‘success’ am I watching too often and too closely?” Perhaps it's worth putting that picture at a distance for a while.

contempt.text: Contempt feels like calm superiority, but behind it there is often an unwillingness to meet what is unlike us. In The Transparency of Evil Baudrillard writes about “radical otherness” — the other who is truly different from us and can't be reduced to our measures. He believed modern culture tolerates it poorly: the other is either made “the same as us” or cast aside. Baudrillard called this “the hell of the same.” From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that contempt is one way of not letting otherness in: the other is declared “lower,” and then you no longer have to reckon with them. The feeling may have its reasons, and there's no need to shame yourself for it. But it is worth asking: what in this person is so foreign to me that it's easier to devalue them than to be surprised by them?
contempt.practice: Name one trait of the person who arouses your contempt that you genuinely don't understand. Try to phrase it as a riddle rather than a flaw.

disgust.text: Disgust — at people, at a situation or at yourself — is a strong bodily “no,” and it is nothing to reproach yourself for. Baudrillard described the modern world as a world of excess: things, images and messages multiply without measure, like “metastases,” and culture reaches a “Xerox degree” — the endless copying of the same thing. He wrote about this with barely hidden disgust at surfeit. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that part of disgust comes not from a particular person but from oversaturation: too much, too close, too alike. Then even your own reflection or other people's faces start to set your teeth on edge. In that case disgust is a signal of “enough,” and it's worth listening to: reduce the flow, step away, give yourself some empty space before judging people.
disgust.practice: Note where today you experienced “too much”: of the feed, of noise, of people. Give yourself ten minutes without screens or new impressions.

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is understandable: you were hurt, and something inside demands an answer. In Symbolic Exchange and Death Baudrillard describes the “symbolic exchange” on which traditional societies rested: a gift demands a counter-gift, a challenge demands a response. Not responding means remaining humiliated. The modern world, for Baudrillard, has largely destroyed this exchange: often there is no one and nothing with which to answer an injury. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that the thirst for revenge is the voice of this ancient need for a response, for restoring balance. It is strong, but it can be quenched not with a blow but with a different kind of answer: naming what happened, defending your boundaries, ending the exchange with the one who wounds you. An answer doesn't have to mirror the injury to give you back your dignity and keep you from being a hostage to someone else's move.
revenge.practice: Write down what “answer” would give you back your sense of dignity. Cross out everything that harms others — what remains?

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at those closest to you — a partner, parents, children — can be especially sharp, and afterward you feel ashamed of it. Baudrillard showed how, in a world of “hyperreality,” images start to seem more real than reality itself. The family has acquired its own simulacra too: perfect family photos, advertising breakfasts, touching posts where no one is ever tired or irritated. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that next to these images, ordinary family anger seems somehow abnormal. But the glossy family is a copy without an original; it doesn't exist. Real close relationships always include irritation, fatigue and conflict. Anger gives no right to wound, but it doesn't mean your family is “worse.” It means this is real life, not a retouched one.
anger_at_loved.practice: Remind yourself: “No family looks like its photos.” Then name one need your anger is signaling.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time being unable to stand them is hard, but it is a very common state. In early works such as For a Critique of the Political Economy of the Sign, Baudrillard contrasted two worlds. The world of the “code” demands unambiguity: every thing and every feeling must have a clear value, plus or minus. The world of “symbolic exchange,” for Baudrillard, is by nature ambivalent: gift and threat, love and rivalry are intertwined, and this doubleness can't be neatly sorted out. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that mixed feelings toward someone close are a sign of a living, symbolic bond, not of something broken. The demand “make up your mind: do you love them or not?” is the demand of the code. A living bond can be warm and painful at once, and it doesn't need to be reduced to a single number.
ambivalence.practice: Describe how you feel about this person without using the words “good” and “bad.” What images, colors or weather suit it?

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, a departure or even the death of a seriously ill loved one can be frightening: “how can I feel this?” Relief and love can exist together. Baudrillard described the “precession of simulacra” — a situation where the model precedes reality: first there is a ready-made image, and then a life that is fitted to it. Loss has its models too — films, rituals, the publicly “correct” reactions: only mourning, only tears. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that shame about relief is often born of a mismatch between a living feeling and the model. But the model is not the measure of truth. Real loss is more complex: it can hold exhaustion from long worry and caregiving, release from pain, gratitude and grief all at once. Relief is part of that complexity, not a betrayal.
guilty_relief.practice: Write down three feelings you have right now, including relief. Notice that they can all be true at the same time.

indifference.text: Sometimes you are untouched by what “should” touch you — and guilt arrives. In the essay In the Shadow of the Silent Majorities Baudrillard wrote about “the masses,” who are endlessly called upon to respond: vote, worry, sympathize, react. And the masses answer with inertia — silence, indifference, absorbing every message without reply. Baudrillard saw in this not dullness but a peculiar defense against endless mobilization. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that your indifference is sometimes the same kind of defense: a psyche overloaded with calls to feel temporarily switches off its response. This doesn't mean you are a cold person. Perhaps you need quiet so that your feelings can come back on their own, without being ordered to.
indifference.practice: Note how many calls to “care” you received over the past day. Give yourself an hour without them and observe what you feel afterward.

escape.text: The urge to drop everything — a job, a city, a role — and go somewhere no one knows you says that life has become too cramped or too noisy. That's understandable. In America Baudrillard describes long drives across the American deserts. For him the desert is a space where familiar meanings, roles and social noise vanish, and you can feel pure speed, light, open space. He wrote about it with a traveler's delight. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that the pull to escape is a longing for such a “desert”: for a place where signs, expectations and roles don't press on you. This desire doesn't necessarily require moving away. Sometimes it's enough to find your own small “desert” — a time and place where for an hour you are free of roles.
escape.practice: This week, find an hour of your own “desert”: a walk without your phone, a road, a quiet place. Notice what changes in you without roles.

forbidden_attraction.text: An attraction you “mustn't” have — to someone unavailable or “the wrong” person — can be confusing and frightening. But a feeling is not an act. In Seduction Baudrillard reminds us that the Latin root of “seduction” means “to lead aside,” to lead off the straight path. He contrasted seduction with “production”: seduction is a play of signs, of the unsaid, of distance, not the uncovering of some “truth of desire.” He even argued with psychoanalysis, which sees in every attraction a secret truth about a person. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that a forbidden attraction doesn't necessarily say “here is your true desire, act on it.” It may be a game that leads you aside from the familiar and shows what you are missing. You can look at it with interest without turning it into either a verdict or a program.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down what this attraction is leading you away from: routine, boredom, loneliness? What does that say about your life right now?

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and their judgment is exhausting: every conversation feels like an exam. Baudrillard showed that in the age of “hyperreality” people increasingly meet each other's images rather than each other: retouched photos, carefully calibrated posts, confident public selves. These images seem more real than the people themselves. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that part of social anxiety comes from comparison: you know your own life from the inside, with all its doubts, while you see others through their smooth simulacra. It seems everyone around is confident and only you are not. But this is a comparison of a living person with a copy without an original. Behind other people's confident images there are also worries, stumbles, awkwardness. You are not the only one who is nervous.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, remind yourself: “Each of them has their own awkwardness that I can't see.” Notice how this changes the feeling in your body.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is hard: you want to know what will happen, and you can't. In late books such as Impossible Exchange, Baudrillard wrote about the “radical uncertainty” of the world: the world can never be fully exchanged for meaning, reduced to a model, a forecast, an explanation. He believed that attempts to calculate and insure against everything only make life more anxious, because uncertainty remains anyway. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that your uncertainty is not a personal failure of planning but a property of the world itself, one everyone faces. This doesn't make the waiting easier, but it relieves you of a task no one can manage: foreseeing everything. You can live inside uncertainty, leaning on what is here now.
uncertainty.practice: Write: “I can't foresee…” and “I can lean on…”. In the second list, include only what you already have today.

waiting.text: Waiting — for results, a reply, news — stretches time, and it's hard to find your place in it. In The Illusion of the End Baudrillard wrote about the culture of “real time”: everything must happen instantly, with no delay, distance or pause. The message has been delivered — so the answer must come now. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that waiting has become especially painful for us precisely because we have lost the habit of waiting: any pause feels like a glitch, a catastrophe. But many things — decisions, results, other people's answers — have their own time, which doesn't match the time of the screen. Waiting is not a breakdown but a return to a human rhythm. You can live through it without checking every minute whether it has arrived yet.
waiting.practice: Choose a stretch of time — say, an hour — during which you don't check whether the reply has come. Spend that time on something slow.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do can return again and again: “what if I had chosen differently?” Baudrillard wrote about simulacra — copies that have no original. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that the “other life” regret paints resembles such a simulacrum. It never existed, and so it is flawless: it has none of the boredom, mistakes and random misfortunes that would have been on the other path too. You are comparing a lived, living life with a perfect copy of what never happened — and the living life loses. It's an unfair comparison. Yet regret can speak of something real: of values that matter to you. You can take them out of the imagined life and begin to live them in the real one, with all its rough edges.
regret.practice: Describe your “unlived life” in three sentences. Then underline the one value in it that matters most to you — and one place where it could appear now.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person — their voice, their smell, their presence — can be almost physical. Baudrillard wrote a great deal about how images and copies replace the real. Today we have photos, videos, messages, video calls — an almost complete illusion of presence. And still the longing doesn't pass. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that longing is precisely the feeling of the reality that can't be simulated: a body present beside you, a shared silence, a touch. A copy can remind you of a person but not replace them. In this sense your longing is not a weakness but faithfulness to the real. You can use images to stay in touch without blaming yourself that they aren't enough: they can't be enough.
longing.practice: Write down exactly what you miss about this person that can't be conveyed through a screen. Think about when and how you might feel it again.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from heavy news, wars, injustice — can weigh you down. It speaks of your sensitivity. In the essay “Requiem for the Media” Baudrillard observed that the media are built as “speech without response”: they talk to us, show us everything, but we can barely answer. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that pain for the world is especially heavy not only because of the events themselves but because of this one-sidedness: you see suffering but can't respond to it. Tension builds up with nowhere to go. That's why it helps to reclaim at least a small response: not just to watch, but to do something — help, support, talk. Even a small response breaks the one-way flow and gives you back your voice.
world_pain.practice: Choose one action with which you can respond to what troubles you in the world — even a small one. Do it, and then set the news aside for a while.

rejection.text: Rejection wounds deeply: it feels as if you were assessed and found insufficient. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard showed how the system turns people and things into sets of signs that can be compared, selected, rejected. Today you can see this, for example, in dating apps and job selection: a decision is made in seconds based on a few features — a photo, a line on a résumé. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that many rejections concern not you but your “sign,” the tiny image that passed through someone else's filter. That image never coincides with the living person. The pain of rejection is real, but it doesn't prove you are “not enough.” What was rejected was a sign, not your complex, real self.
rejection.practice: Write down what exactly was “seen” of you in the rejection — a few features. Then add three things about yourself that no filter could have seen.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned is exhausting: you catch every sign and dread every pause. This fear often grows from old wounds and deserves gentleness. In The System of Objects Baudrillard writes about collecting. He notes that objects also attract us because they can be completely controlled: a collection will never leave, never fall out of love, never abandon you. Through objects a person tries to cope with the fear of loss. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that the fear of being abandoned is the other side of the fact that a living person will never become an “object” in our collection. They are free — and so they can leave. But that is exactly why their presence beside you is not possession but a choice they make. You can notice that choice and value it.
abandonment.practice: Recall one recent moment when someone close chose to be with you. Describe it in a single sentence.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love wounds deeply: you give your feeling, and there is no answer. In Fatal Strategies Baudrillard offers an unexpected view: we usually think that the subject — the one who desires — is in charge, and the object is passive. But Baudrillard shows that the object is often stronger: it slips away, doesn't respond, remains impenetrable, and precisely by doing so holds our attention. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that in unrequited love the other is not “to blame” and not “cruel”: they simply remain other and don't submit to our desire. This is hard to accept, but it frees you from the endless attempt to “earn” an answer. Your feeling is real and valuable, but you are not obliged to pursue someone who remains beyond your power.
unrequited.practice: Tell yourself: “They are free not to answer. I am free not to pursue.” Notice what you felt.

humiliation.text: Humiliation is one of the most painful experiences: you want the scene erased from memory, yours and everyone else's. Baudrillard wrote about the “transparency” of the modern world: everything must be visible; everything is recorded, forwarded, discussed. An awkward moment can turn into a picture that lives separately from you. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that a humiliating scene, especially one many people saw, turns into a simulacrum — an image that seems more real than you yourself. But it is a copy of a single moment cut out of a life. You are not that scene. You have a past before it and a future after it that the image can't contain. In time, other people's attention moves on to new pictures, and you remain yourself.
humiliation.practice: Write: “This scene is one frame from my life. What it doesn't show is…” and add three important things about yourself that the frame doesn't show.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body can be quiet and constant, and it deserves care. Symbolic Exchange and Death has a chapter called “The Body, or the Mass Grave of Signs.” Baudrillard shows how fashion and advertising cut the body into separate “parts-as-signs”: lips, legs, belly, skin — each part must meet a standard and is judged separately. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that body shame often works the same way: you look not at yourself as a whole but at a “detail” that “falls short.” But the body is not a set of signs; it is a living whole that breathes, moves, feels and holds you in the world. You can return from examining parts to sensing yourself as a whole.
body_shame.practice: Close your eyes and feel your whole body, from the crown of your head to your feet, as one. Notice one sensation that feels pleasant.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, it is hard both physically and emotionally: plans fall apart, and you have to depend on others. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard wrote about the “cult of health”: health becomes not simply a good but an obligation and a status symbol. A healthy, toned, energetic body is the mark of a successful person. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that in such a world illness is experienced not only as suffering but as a “failure,” a shameful defeat. This adds extra weight to what is already hard. But illness is not a failure or a sign of your inadequacy. It is part of human life, something that happens to all bodies. You can release yourself from the demand to “keep it together” and let yourself simply be ill and take care of yourself.
illness.practice: Tell yourself: “There is no shame in being ill.” Choose one small act of self-care for today — without any demand to be productive.

pride.text: Pride in what you've done is a healthy, well-earned feeling, and it is worth enjoying. In The System of Objects Baudrillard compares mass-produced, assembly-line objects with antique, handmade ones. An antique object, he observes, has a special value: you can see in it “the trace of the hand,” the imprint of the person who made it. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that healthy pride is joy in such a trace: not in a “status symbol” that can be bought, but in having made something yourself, having put in time, effort and attention. Such pride can't be faked or purchased. It needs no display or likes, though sharing it with people close to you is good too. You can simply look at what you've made and recognize your own hand in it.
pride.practice: Look at what you are proud of and find in it “the trace of your hand” — a detail that exists only because you in particular made it.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness is a quiet, tender feeling with no misfortune in it. It doesn't need “fixing.” In the final chapter of Simulacra and Simulation Baudrillard wrote about melancholy as the general mood of the era: a world where meanings dissolve in a stream of images is tinged with quiet sadness. He said this about culture, not about individuals, but something warm can be drawn from his thought. From Baudrillard's point of view, you could say that a personal, gentle melancholy is a way of feeling the real amid the gloss. It doesn't put on a brave face or fake positivity, and it lets you notice fragility, time gone by, real losses. In this sense melancholy is an honest feeling. You can live through it without shame, allowing yourself a little silence and shadow.
melancholy.practice: Choose a place or activity that brings you a gentle sadness. Spend a few minutes there without your phone.
